title: Founder's bookshelf
note: Four books distilled by theme, each idea credited: Ready, Fire, Aim (Michael Masterson), The Effective Executive (Peter F. Drucker), The Ideal Team Player (Patrick Lencioni), Scaling People (Claire Hughes Johnson). Built from the chapter summaries listed below, not the books' text; stories and outside commentary left out.

concepts.s: Masterson: every business passes four revenue stages, each with its own problem, challenge and opportunity, and you only need the skills of the stage you are in.

x.b:
1. Infancy, $0–1M (1–8 people): problem: you don't know what you're doing. Challenge: the first profitable sale. Opportunity: a critical mass of customers.
  2. Fast growth, $1–10M (9–50): problem: breaking even or losing money. Challenge: more profitable products. Opportunity: profit through constant innovation.
  3. Adolescence, $10–50M (51–350): problem: systems break and customers notice. Challenge: chaos to order. Opportunity: protocols and systems that work.
  4. Maturity, $50M+ (350+): problem: sales slow or plateau. Challenge: become entrepreneurial again. Opportunity: a business that runs itself.

• Stage 1: get going and sell.
  • Stage 2: + create new products.
  • Stage 3: + manage well.
  • Stage 4: + hire superstars.
  • No natural talent needed: know which problem to work on now.

cards.q: Masterson's four stages and revenue bands?
cards.a: Infancy $0–1M, fast growth $1–10M, adolescence $10–50M, maturity $50M+.
Create more profitable products.
Systems strain and customers notice; turn chaos into order.
Become entrepreneurial again as growth plateaus.

concepts.s: Masterson: in infancy selling is everything, so spend 80% of your time finding an Optimal Selling Strategy and defer everything else.

x.b:
The best way to acquire customers: usually your competitors' mix of media, price and positioning plus one unique element. Answer four questions:

  1. Where are the customers? Copy how established players acquire them. A mediocre ad in the best place beats a brilliant one nobody sees.
  2. What product first? Something that already sells, or a better me-too of what is hot. Don't expect the market to change for you.
  3. What price? About the competitor's. Undercutting signals inferiority; raise prices later; make money on the back end.
  4. How to persuade? Test 2–3 copy versions, 2–3 prices, 2 platforms. Hire an experienced copywriter.

1. List features, then every benefit.
  2. Tie a benefit to a rising trend.
  3. Write several USPs; test them on prospects.
  4. Turn the best USP into a Big Idea with a Big Promise and proof for each claim.
  5. Test two or more ads, roll out the winner, repeat.

• Defer logos, brochures, offices, hiring and paperwork.
  • Get a mentor; keep a small team of generalists who think like marketers.
  • Write revenue and profit targets and share them.
  • Direct marketing only: watch what people buy, not what they say in surveys.
  • Listen to people who have done it, not consultants.
  • Critical mass: know what a customer is worth over their lifetime, spend up to that to acquire them, and use a cheap lead product.
Trap: Thinking you know more than the market. Test before you commit.

cards.q: Share of founder time on selling in stage 1?

cards.a: Where are the customers, what product first, what price, how to persuade.

cards.q: How should a stage-1 product be priced?
cards.a: About what competitors charge; undercutting signals an inferior product.
It shows what people do, not what they say.

concepts.s: Masterson: past $1M, escape the one-product trap by launching many profitable variations quickly; growth is innovation times speed squared.

x.b:
• Most stage-1 firms live on one product; a one-shot company stalls.
  • Grow the front end (new customers) and the back end (more products for existing customers) at once.
  • Innovate by variation: improve what sells or out-do the hottest product; ride fast-growing trends. Breakthroughs are not required.
  • Rule of thumb: 80% of stage-2 growth = Innovation × Speed².

• One step removed: build on what you already do well.
  • Product cube: price (cheap, moderate, expensive) × service (self-help, assisted, managed) × type (product, service, add-on).
  • A rotating executive brainstorming team; beta-test with existing customers; fail faster.

cards.a: 80% of growth = Innovation × Speed².
Front: selling to new customers. Back: more products to existing ones.

cards.q: What are the three axes of the product cube?
cards.a: Price, service level, and type (product, service, add-on).

concepts.s: Masterson: answer seven questions, launch within days, then improve what sells; perfectionism kills more ideas than speed.

x.b:
1. Is it a good idea?
  2. Does my gut say it will work?
  3. Are targets realistic, and does it still pay at double the cost and half the sales?
  4. Can we afford a small test?
  5. Is it within our capabilities?
  6. Do we have the people: a champion, sellers, fulfilment?
  7. Is there a Plan B with a written stop-loss?

Write it as a 1–4 page proposal in under 24 hours: rough numbers, critical tasks, champion and team, timeline, Plan B. Brevity is the soul of velocity.

• Fire: start while enthusiastic; launch imperfect; don't let chores or perfectionism stall it.
  • Speed raises quality: less money goes into features customers don't care about, more into aim.
  • Aim: drop what doesn't sell; improve in small steps, not relaunches; offer past buyers an upgrade; then fine-tune the marketing.
Trap: Fire-at-will: launching without the seven ready questions.

cards.q: What test must a Masterson project pass on numbers?
cards.a: It still makes money at double the costs and half the sales.

cards.q: How long and how big is a ready-fire-aim proposal?
cards.a: Under 24 hours to write, 1–4 pages.

cards.q: Why does speed improve quality, per Masterson?
cards.a: Less money goes into features customers don't value, leaving more to improve what sells.

cards.q: What must every launch have before firing?
cards.a: A champion and a Plan B with a written stop-loss.

concepts.s: Masterson: you can only sell to more people, sell more to the people you have, or charge more, so organize marketing around all three.

x.b:
• More people: new lead products and niches; best marketers on the front end.
  • More per customer: a second team on the back end.
  • Higher price: premium positioning.

• Find the big spenders: 20% of customers make 80% of profit.
  • Make the add-on offer right after the first purchase, while the buying frenzy lasts.
  • Appeal to desires, not needs; make repeat purchases automatic (bill till forbid); treat the best customers as VIPs; never leave a dead end.

• Customers care about themselves, not you; learn why they buy and what they fear and want.
  • A USP for every product and an identity for every line.
  • Big Idea + Big Benefit + Big Promise + proof.
  • Track every initiative separately; learn from complaints.
  • Give before you ask; pre-qualify; never push or bribe; sell with confidence and real value.

cards.q: Masterson's three ways to grow revenue?
cards.a: Sell to more people, sell more to existing customers, charge more.

cards.q: When to make the back-end offer?
cards.a: Right after the first purchase.
Bill till forbid: continuity until the customer cancels.

concepts.s: Masterson: past $10M the business outgrows you, so hire professionals, build stars and superstars, and stop being the bottleneck.

x.b:
• CEO over a COO for operations and a manager per product-line profit center; each hires marketing, sales and product-development leads.
  • CEO: six or fewer direct reports; most time on marketing and product development.

• Become a corporate leader: work through others, communicate the vision, network for joint ventures, negotiate.
  • Hire and keep stars (do what you ask) and superstars (also create growth); mentor a few very good people into superstars.

• Don't be the bottleneck: hire great people and get out of their way.
  • Add a legal function for compliance.
  • Cut procedures that slow you; build efficiency.
  • Kill fiefdoms; best idea wins.
  • Put almost no limits on product development and marketing.
  • The road to $100M: joint ventures and superstars who become intrapreneurs.

cards.a: A star does what you ask; a superstar also creates growth.

cards.q: CEO's span and focus in stage 3?
cards.a: Six or fewer reports; most time on marketing and product development.
Joint ventures and superstars turned intrapreneurs.

concepts.s: Masterson: at maturity the founder's best role is wealth builder: step back to adviser, let managers run it, and reinvest the profits.

x.b:
• Employee: you become a bottleneck.
  • Manager: you distract the profit-center heads.
  • Business builder: your ideas get harder to apply.
  • Wealth builder: grow the company's value as an asset. The right role.

• Step down as CEO; advise, and accept managers may ignore you. You add value by doing less (Buffett at Berkshire).
  • Keep growing through joint ventures and acquisitions; buy only what you know, with a Plan B.
  • Selling privately: you'd be bored in six months; keep ownership instead.
  • Go public only if there is no other way to fund growth.

cards.q: Masterson's best role for a stage-4 founder?
cards.a: Wealth builder: adviser and investor, not operator.

cards.q: When does Masterson say to go public?
cards.a: Only if there is no other way to fund growth.

cards.q: Why keep the business rather than sell it?
cards.a: You'd likely be bored in six months; stay as owner-adviser.

concepts.s: Drucker: effectiveness, getting the right things done, is a set of five learnable habits, not a personality or talent.

x.b:
• An executive is any knowledge worker responsible for a contribution that materially affects results and who must make decisions, managing people or not.
  • Intelligence, imagination and knowledge are only resources; effectiveness turns them into results.
  • Four realities pull you toward non-results: your time belongs to everyone; you keep operating unless you act; you are effective only if others use your output; results exist only outside the organization.

1. Know where your time goes.
  2. Focus on outward contribution.
  3. Build on strengths.
  4. Concentrate on the few areas where superior performance yields outstanding results.
  5. Make few, fundamental decisions based on dissent.

Drucker's later introduction adds:

  1. Ask what needs to be done.
  2. Ask what is right for the enterprise.
  3. Write action plans (intentions, revised often).
  4. Take responsibility for decisions.
  5. Take responsibility for communicating.
  6. Focus on opportunities, not problems.
  7. Run productive meetings.
  8. Think and say we, not I.

Plus: listen first, speak last.

cards.a: A knowledge worker responsible for a contribution that materially affects results, who must make decisions.
Know your time, focus on contribution, build on strengths, concentrate, decide effectively.
Learned, not taught: it is a self-discipline built by practice.

cards.q: What is the last of the eight practices?
cards.a: Think and say we, not I.

concepts.s: Drucker: start with time, not tasks; record it as it is spent, cut what wastes it, and consolidate the rest into large blocks.

x.b:
1. Record in real time, never from memory: 3–4 weeks, twice a year.
  2. Manage: ask of each item: what if this were not done at all? (cut about a quarter); who else could do it as well or better?; ask others what of yours wastes their time.
  3. Consolidate discretionary time: a quarter of a day in large blocks beats three quarters in fragments. Use fixed meeting days or home mornings, and keep pruning.

1. No system or foresight: a recurring crisis should be foreseen and made routine.
  2. Overstaffing: seniors spend real time on people friction.
  3. Malorganization: too many meetings; over a quarter of time in meetings is the sign.
  4. Malfunctioning information.

Important work (people decisions, reports, time with knowledge workers) needs large uninterrupted blocks; minutes with people are unproductive.

cards.a: Record, manage, consolidate.

cards.q: First diagnostic question for each activity?
cards.a: What would happen if this were not done at all?
Lack of system or foresight.

cards.q: How much of the time log can usually go?
cards.a: About a quarter.

concepts.s: Drucker: ask what you can contribute that significantly changes the organization's results, and judge yourself by output, not effort or authority.

x.b:
• Whoever takes responsibility for results is top management, whatever the rank.
  • Three performance areas, all required: direct results; building and reaffirming values; developing people for tomorrow.
  • Redefine your contribution in every new job.
  • Specialists must make themselves understood and ask who uses their output.

• The four requirements of good human relations: communication, teamwork, self-development, developing others.
  • People grow to the demands made on them.
  • State the purpose and expected contribution at the start of every meeting and report.

cards.a: What can I contribute that will significantly affect results?
Direct results, values, developing people.

cards.q: The four requirements of good human relations?
cards.a: Communication, teamwork, self-development, developing others.

concepts.s: Drucker: concentration is the one secret of effectiveness: first things first, one at a time, second things not at all.

x.b:
• Commit to nothing beyond the current task, then reassess.
  • Slough off yesterday: if we weren't already doing this, would we start? Drop an old activity before adding a new one.
  • Give new tasks to proven people.
  • Posteriorities, what not to tackle, are the hard part; what you postpone you abandon.
  • Ask who sets priorities: you or the pressures.

• Future over past.
  • Opportunity over problem.
  • Your own direction over the bandwagon.
  • Aim high for what makes a difference.

• Treat change as opportunity; put opportunities on page one of reports.
  • Every six months list opportunities and your best people, and match them.

cards.a: Concentration: first things first, one at a time.
What you decide not to tackle.
If we weren't already doing this, would we start now?
Proven performers, not new hires.

concepts.s: Drucker: make few, important decisions at the level of principle by five steps: classify, specify, find what's right, build in action, get feedback.

x.b:
1. Classify: generic problems get a rule or policy; true exceptions are handled on their merits. A seeming one-off may be the first sign of a new generic problem.
  2. Boundary conditions: what the decision must achieve. Drop the decision when they change.
  3. What's right before what's acceptable: half a loaf is a fair compromise, half a baby is not.
  4. Build in action: who must know, what action, by whom; rewards must not contradict it. A decision is a good intention until it degenerates into work.
  5. Feedback: test against events; go and look yourself.

Trap: Treating a generic situation as a string of unique events, or a new event as an old one.
Trap: Temporary decisions tend to become permanent.

cards.a: Classify: generic or exceptional.

cards.q: Half a loaf vs half a baby?
cards.a: A partial win that still works vs a compromise that destroys the purpose.

cards.q: When is a decision really made?
cards.a: When it has been built into action: who acts, by when, and who must know.

concepts.s: Drucker: a decision is a judgment between alternatives, so start from opinions, demand dissent, and decide only when acting beats not acting.

x.b:
• Start with opinions as untested hypotheses; ask each holder what the test against reality must show.
  • Find the right measurement; assume the traditional one is wrong.
  • No decision without disagreement. Dissent frees you from the organization, provides alternatives and stimulates imagination.
  • Find out why people disagree, not who is right.

• Act if things will degenerate or an opportunity will be lost; don't if it will take care of itself.
  • Act or don't; never hedge or half-act.
  • Refuse "let's study it again"; wait only briefly if uneasy.

• Review them at a pre-agreed time. If one failed, the decider erred.
  • Don't keep non-performers in important jobs; offer a return to the old job.

cards.q: What should a decision start from?
cards.a: Opinions treated as hypotheses to test.
Keeps you from being captive, provides alternatives, stimulates imagination.
Act or don't; never hedge.

cards.q: Who erred when a promotion fails?
cards.a: The person who made the decision.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson: managers run on four principles that build trust: self-awareness, candor, knowing managing from leading, and returning to the operating system.

x.b:
1. Build self-awareness to build mutual awareness (values, work style, skills).
  2. Say the thing you think you cannot say.
  3. Distinguish management (execution, stability) from leadership (vision, change).
  4. Come back to the operating system: consistency lets people predict you.

• Each principle protects trust; be the honest broker for your team.
  • Vulnerability builds trust but needs a relationship first; show it yourself.
  • Openness is negotiable, honesty is not: share what people need to do their best work, and set expectations for what is shared.

cards.a: Self-awareness, say the unsayable, management vs leadership, return to the operating system.
Openness is negotiable; honesty is not.
Management is execution and stability; leadership is vision and change.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson: write down the mission, long-term goals and values, plus a charter per team, because past about 50 people they become the touchstones.

x.b:
• Mission: specific enough that no other company could use it, ambitious enough that it may never be finished; often discovered, not forced.
  • Long-term goals: concrete; annual and quarterly goals ladder up to them.
  • Values: authentic, tested with employees, used in hiring, reviews and daily work.
  • Team charters: purpose, goals, responsibilities, metrics, accountability.
  • An honest culture guide that includes the hard parts.
• Most of this is premature before product-market fit, but state the mission early for recruits and investors.

cards.q: When do founding documents become touchstones?
cards.a: Past roughly 40–50 people.
No other company could use it, and it may never be fully achieved.

cards.q: What does a team charter contain?
cards.a: Purpose, long-term goals, responsibilities, metrics, accountability.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson: run the company on visible norms for strategy, goals, metrics, accountability and a steady cadence.

x.b:
• Strategy is resource allocation across bets, balancing new against the proven core. A strategy should hurt.
  • Metrics at every level, short and long term, tied to goals.
  • Accountability: clear owners, weekly team reviews, quarterly business reviews.
  • Communication: documented, accessible, candid.
  • Cadence: a standard rhythm for reporting and decisions. Have a cadence but don't get stuck in it.

• Keep the rules, score and constraints visible, especially when the plan changes.
  • Align structure to strategy; never restructure reactively or around individuals.

cards.q: What is strategy, per Hughes Johnson?
cards.a: Allocating people and money across growth bets.
Hurt: it says no to things.
Align it to strategy; never react or build around individuals.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson: most teams are only groups, so build habits, structure and safety deliberately, and delegate by how reversible a decision is.

x.b:
• Teams have an ongoing mission; projects and working groups are temporary.
  • Diagnose each member's history, aspirations and skills.
  • Structure teams to fit short- and long-term strategy; manage dependencies with shared planning.
  • Multi-product firms need hinge roles (product marketing, specialist sales) or they ship their org chart.
  • Meetings need agendas, goals and roles; offsites build strategy and trust; psychological safety comes first.

• Low skill: train or hire.
  • Too much skill: raise the challenge.
  • Low will: reconnect to the mission.
  • Too much will: set explicit expectations.

• Keep only high-stakes, irreversible calls; delegate the rest. Over- and under-delegating both hurt.
  • Founders must give away their Legos as they scale.

cards.a: A team has habits and processes that make the whole exceed the parts; a group just shares a manager.

cards.q: Skill-will: what to do with low will?
cards.a: Reconnect the person to the mission.

cards.q: What should a leader keep rather than delegate?
cards.a: High-stakes, irreversible decisions.

concepts.s: Drucker: staff for what people do uncommonly well and make their weaknesses irrelevant; staffing to avoid weakness yields mediocrity.

x.b:
1. A job that defeats two or three good people in a row is badly designed: redesign it.
  2. Make every job big and demanding.
  3. Start from what a person can do; appraise performance and strengths, not potential.
  4. Accept weaknesses to get strengths, but never a lack of integrity.

• Ask "what can they do uncommonly well?", not "how do they get along with me?"
  • Design jobs by task, not personality.
  • Remove people who consistently fail.
  • Make your boss's strengths productive; don't try to reform the boss.
  • Know your own strengths and way of working.

cards.q: Drucker's test for an impossible job?
cards.a: It defeated two or three good people in a row.

cards.q: What does staffing to avoid weakness produce?
cards.a: Mediocrity at best.

cards.q: What weakness should never be accepted?
cards.a: Lack of character or integrity.
Make their strengths productive.

concepts.s: Lencioni: the ideal team player has all three virtues; missing one makes teamwork hard, and humility matters most.

x.b:
• Humble: little ego, shares credit, admits mistakes. The deepest virtue. Beware both the arrogant and the insecure who undervalue themselves.
  • Hungry: self-motivated, always wants more work, learning and responsibility; rarely needs pushing.
  • Smart: people sense, not intellect: reads others, listens, knows the effect of their words.
  • Adequate levels of all three are enough; the virtues can be learned.

• Humble only: pawn. Hungry only: bulldozer. Smart only: charmer.
  • Humble + hungry: accidental mess-maker.
  • Humble + smart: lovable slacker.
  • Hungry + smart: skillful politician, the most dangerous because hardest to spot.
  • Anyone missing a virtue takes far more of a manager's time.

cards.a: Humble.
Skillful politician.
Accidental mess-maker.
Lovable slacker.
People sense, not intellect.

concepts.s: Lencioni and Hughes Johnson: treat hiring as a structured, data-driven process aimed at specific virtues, and never lower the bar to fill a seat.

x.b:
• Generic interviews reveal little; target each virtue.
  • Debrief as a team right after each interview; use group interviews and non-traditional settings such as an errand.
  • Ask questions more than once, and ask what others would say about the candidate.
  • Have them do real work; ask junior staff how they were treated; check references on attitude.
  • Investigate every doubt; tell candidates plainly you hire for humble, hungry, smart.
  • Three who fit beat four with one who doesn't.

• Treat recruiting like sales: brand, funnel, conversion; build the pipeline ahead of need.
  • Honest job descriptions; one rubric; several trained interviewers; the hiring manager decides.
  • Founders interview and act as bar raiser as long as possible.
  • Onboard on mission, values and people; measure ramp time.
  • Fix hiring mistakes fast, then run a retrospective.

• Humble: we over I; owning a mistake.
  • Hungry: the hardest they've worked.
  • Smart: how they treat everyone, all day.

cards.a: Right after each one, as a team.

cards.q: Why ask what others would say about the candidate?
cards.a: It gets past rehearsed self-descriptions.

cards.q: Who makes the hire, per Hughes Johnson?
cards.a: The hiring manager, after hearing the committee.

cards.q: What to do with a hiring mistake?
cards.a: Fix it fast, then run a retrospective.

concepts.s: Lencioni: assess everyone on the three virtues, coach the gaps week after week, and make teamwork the explicit, enforced culture.

x.b:
• Qualitative, virtue by virtue: manager questions, self-ratings, peer discussion.
  • Three outcomes: confirm, develop, or move out. Keeping misfits is cruel; they are the unhappiest people there.
  • If nobody leaves or is asked to leave, you're not living the values.

• Name the gap; manager and employee work on it together; remind and coach weekly. They break through or opt out.
  • Humble: practice it before it feels natural.
  • Hungry: tie them to the mission; set and hold expectations.
  • Smart: blunt, kind, repeated feedback on specific behaviors.

• Leaders must commit first and live it.
  • Say it explicitly to staff, partners and customers.
  • Catch and revere: praise teamwork on the spot; address violations promptly and kindly.
  • Build it into recruiting and reviews.
  • Team exercise: each names their strongest and weakest virtue, leader first.
  • Lack of humility kills the trust the Five Dysfunctions model depends on.

cards.a: Confirm, develop, or move out.
Blunt, kind, repeated feedback on specific behaviors.

cards.q: Sign you aren't living the values?
cards.a: No one leaves or is asked to leave.
Praise teamwork on the spot so everyone sees it.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson: give feedback continuously by hypothesis, run fair formal reviews too, and act decisively on high and low performers.

x.b:
• Avoid both the extreme coach and the forgot-to coach; don't save feedback for reviews.
  • Hypothesis-based: observe across situations, form a hypothesis, test it in conversation, say it before you feel ready.
  • Open with questions; describe behavior and impact, not the person; solve jointly.
  • Praise in public, criticize in private; ask for feedback on yourself.

• Announce process and criteria in advance; inputs: self-assessment, selected peers, manager.
  • Five-point scale from does not meet to greatly exceeds; calibrate across managers and groups for bias.
  • Pay by a written compensation philosophy.
  • High performers: stretch and recognize. Low performers: documented conversations, then a plan or exit, handled respectfully.

cards.a: Observe, form a hypothesis, test it in conversation, say it before you feel ready.
Self-assessment, peers, manager.
To catch bias and leniency across managers and groups.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson and Drucker: your own self-management sets your team's ceiling, so know your strengths, guard your energy and time, and grow with your role.

x.b:
• Hughes Johnson: track what gives and drains energy; work in peak hours; set boundaries.
  • Protect important-but-not-urgent work (Eisenhower matrix).
  • Your strengths are also sources of weakness.
  • Be your own career coach: hard skills, then soft skills, then how you show up emotionally.
  • Ask for help; keep mistakes in perspective; build ties with your manager, peers and mentors.
  • Scale to the call: grow as fast as your role.
  • Drucker: know your strengths and the way you work best, and let others work their way.

cards.a: Your own self-management.
Hard skills, then soft skills, then how you show up emotionally.
Grow as fast as your role grows.
